pr_title: Optimizer: Fix range intersection for CNF(conjunctive normal form)  | tidb-test=pr/2350
pr_body:
<!--

Thank you for contributing to TiDB!

PR Title Format:
1. pkg [, pkg2, pkg3]: what's changed
2. *: what's changed

-->

### What problem does this PR solve?
<!--

Please create an issue first to describe the problem.

There MUST be one line starting with "Issue Number:  " and
linking the relevant issues via the "close" or "ref".

For more info, check https://pingcap.github.io/tidb-dev-guide/contribute-to-tidb/contribute-code.html#referring-to-an-issue.

-->

Issue Number: close #54337

### Problem Summary:
Current code does not optimally find index range when we have the filter as complex conjuncts. A complex cojunct in this context is DNF. The code does well for each DNF and builds a union of ranges but for the CNF part, it does not do full intersection. The code does intersection only for point ranges which may not as selective as the full intersection.  There is a simple example under https://github.com/tikv/tikv/issues/16798 that shows the optimization limitation. 

### What changed and how does it work?
 We added code  does full intersection of ranges. For example, if we have ((a1>1) or (a1=1 and b1 > 10)) and ((a1<10) or (a1=10 and b1 < 20))
then there are two conjuncts : 
- ((a1>1) or (a1=1 and b1 > 10)) 
- ((a1<10) or (a1=10 and b1 < 20))
The first produces intervals : (1 10,1 +inf], (1,+inf] and second intervals is [-inf,10), [10 -inf,10 20) and their intersection is 
(1 10,1 +inf], (1,10), [10 -inf,10 20).  Before this fix, the code just produce point ranges as [10,10], (1,1].

issue_context.body:
## Enhancement
This issue is covered in details under https://github.com/tikv/tikv/issues/16798 which is listed under TiKV.
The enhancement here belongs to the optimizer and we created this issue to track it. Please refer to https://github.com/tikv/tikv/issues/16798 for the details of the problem. 

For completeness, see the first comment below repeated from the original PR.
comments:
Q1 is ((a1>1) or (a1=1 and b1 > 10)) and we get the correct range:(1 10,1 +inf], (1,+inf]
Q2 is ((a1<10) or (a1=10 and b1 < 20)) and we also get the correct range:[-inf,10), [10 -inf,10 20)
Q3 is Q1 and Q2 combined. ((a1>1) or (a1=1 and b1 > 10)) and ((a1<10) or (a1=10 and b1 < 20)) and we get correct intersection but not optimal range:[1,1], (1,10), [10,10]
Correct result for Q3 is Q4 with range range:(1 10,1 +inf], (1,10), [10 -inf,10 20)

review_comments: Ideally, we can order the two `Ranges` and avoid calculating the intersection for every pair between them, right?
Correct and that will be done in subsequent PR when we optimize the intersections and remove the flag.
What does `low1` and `low2` mean here?
The comment says about what type of bound which lower or upper and that is covered in low1, low2. I added more text to the comemnt.

Could you add some examples for this function here, or in the code below?
I think it's hard for one at first sight to grasp the idea behind `open1`, `open2`, `low1`, and `low2`, and how these values lead to different results.

The test cases cover these combinations. I do not think it is a good idea to add examples as comments unless it is something simple and not covering combinations like this. We should have comments in the code and I hope I did that. The logic is no complicated. If one value is not equal to the other in the suffix then it is simple. The extra logic for cases where they are equal in the common length and it goes through cases of n1 == n2, n1 > n2 and n1 < n2. For each case, there is additional logic for lower/upper bounds.
It seems different `open1` should result in different results.
it will be the same here if it is open or close because it is -infinity. -infinity is lower than any other value.

It becomes a bit complicated here and I think it relates to the definition of what a range with fewer columns means.
I come up with one example: `[1 1,1 5) [1 5 1,1 6 5]`. I think `1 5)` should be less than `[1 5 1` because the first range should come from expressions like `a = 1 and b >= 1 and b < 5`.
Looks like the key issue here is that does `[1 1,1 5)` mean `a = 1 and b >= 1 and b < 5` or `a = 1 and b >= 1 and b < 6`.

The example above is not applicable, You are using a general n dimensional range and not the lexiographically ordered index. [1 5 1,1 6 5] is not a valid index range. All the prefix should be single point. The open and closed is applied to all the columns. So do you mean (1 5 compared to [1 5 1, yes it is less than and consistent with the code.  [1 5 is also less than (1 5 1 and same for other combinations. If you mean comparing the upper bound 1 5) to lower bound [1 5 1 then you are comparing 1 5 +infinity) and [1 5 1 and  1 5 +infinity)  is higher.
[1 1,1 5) mean a = 1 and b >= 1 and b < 5 and this is consistent the general math open/closed interval semantics.

> [1 5 1,1 6 5] is not a valid index range

This can be a valid range. If the user writes`(a,b,c) >= (1,5,1) and (a,b,c) <= (1,6,5)`, that's exactly what we want.

> If you mean comparing the upper bound 1 5) to lower bound [1 5 1 then you are comparing 1 5 +infinity) and [1 5 1 and 1 5 +infinity) is higher.

If `[1 1,1 5)` means `a = 1 and b >= 1 and b < 5`, then `1 5)` means `1 5 -infinity)` instead of `1 5 +infinity)`, right? Because `a = 1 and b = 5 and c = -999` doesn't satisfy `a = 1 and b >= 1 and b < 5`.
Then `1 5)` should be lower than `[1 5 1`.

1 5) as an upper bound means a=1 and b < 5 and c anything which means c < +infinity. If you take a simple example of [1 5, 1 5] it means a=1 and b=1 and all values of c which means c >= -infinity for low range and c <= +infinity for the upper bound.

This comment and subsequent ones are about returning results rather than storing the result with a single return at the end. It is style issue and not sure which one is better. In this case, I find the single return is more readable code given that there are multiple cases where we need to run the heuristic. In any case, I would rather keep it like this and avoid the code for the case rangeResult == nil.
Ditto. Looks like we can directly return here.
